criteria.note: The core answer to 'where is the gluten in Korean food' — the fermented condiments — lands in the second paragraph, well inside 200 words, and the condiment table follows immediately.
Title is 35 chars (55 with the rendered ' | Gluten-Free Korea' suffix), description is ~153 chars, and the keyword appears naturally in both without the description echoing the title's framing.

Headings carry the argument rather than label sections — a skim of 'The fermented condiment problem', 'The allergen line only covers wheat', 'Noodles: mostly wheat, with two bright spots', 'The good news: control the condiments' reconstructs the whole thesis.
Four distinct internal destinations (label-reading guide, restaurant list, celiac travel guide) each placed where a reader would actually need the next step.
All three FAQ answers — soy sauce, tteokbokki, dangmyeon — are directly supported by the condiment table, the 밀떡 correction and the noodles section, and each reads standalone.
Named places and specific failures: a named anchor restaurant closing, a loaf silently renamed after purchase, a shop visited in Yeonnam, and an explicit correction of the author's own earlier error.
Korean terms are consistently romanised and glossed, a specific product line (양조간장 501) and the exact regulatory instrument (식품등의 표시기준 별표 2) are cited precisely enough to check.
Both load-bearing claims point to primary sources — the manufacturer's own product page and the MFDS labeling standard — each with a retrieval date and a note that the standard is amended.
A dedicated scope paragraph states what label-reading cannot establish, unverified leads are flagged as leads, and no commercial link appears anywhere in the piece.

findings.quote: **Soy sauce → imported Japanese tamari.** The easiest wheat-free substitute to find in Seoul; Lotte Mart, the larger Emart branches and Kim's Club carry it.
findings.why: The single most actionable recommendation in the piece names a category and three retailers but no product a reader could pick off the shelf, while the rest of the article insists the answer is set by the product and not the brand. It leaves the strongest 'what do I actually buy' query only half-answered.
findings.fix: Name the specific tamari and gluten-free gochujang currently in the kitchen, with the 원재료명 line you verified and the month you checked it — matching the treatment given to Sempio 501.

findings.quote: Usually not, and the rice cakes are only part of the answer. Tteokbokki tteok comes as 쌀떡 (rice) or 밀떡 (mil-tteok), which is made with wheat flour and is entirely mainstream
findings.why: All three FAQ answers run 80-120 words. They are fully supported by the body, but at that length a rich result will truncate mid-sentence and the load-bearing caveat (cross-contamination, mixed-starch dangmyeon) sits past the cut.
findings.fix: Front-load a 1-2 sentence direct answer in each FAQ entry, then keep the detail — so the truncated snippet still carries the verdict.

findings.quote: **For a trip → monil2 house** in Yeonnam sells travel-sized packets of gluten-free gochujang and soy sauce
findings.why: A named shop is recommended by name and neighbourhood with no statement of relationship. There is no link and no sign of an affiliate arrangement, but readers cannot tell that from the page, and the piece otherwise discloses its limits carefully.
findings.fix: Add a one-line note that the site takes no payment or product from shops it names, either inline or in the scope paragraph near the top.

findings.quote: **We went looking for a Korean equivalent of [GFCO](https://gfco.org)** — a third-party body that audits a facility and licenses a seal — and as of August 2026 we have not found one.
findings.why: The GFCO link is the only outbound reference without a retrieval date, and the surrounding claim is a negative finding about the Korean market that carries real weight for readers deciding whether to trust a front-of-package claim.
findings.fix: Date the GFCO reference like the others, and state briefly what was searched (MFDS certification registry, KFDA scheme names) so the absence is auditable.

criteria.note: Central claims are sourced to the manufacturer and the MFDS standard or explicitly marked as personal observation, but several category-level statements in the second-tier list are neither, though all point in the conservative direction.
criteria.evidence_quote: **카레 루 (*kare-ru*, curry roux)** — Japanese-style Korean curry blocks are thickened with wheat flour.

criteria.note: Product names, the linked manufacturer page, the regulatory citation and all dates are checkable and internally consistent, no statistics are invented, and the update note discloses that an unsourceable percentage figure was removed.

The piece states its basis is reading 원재료명 on products the authors cook with plus linked sources, explicitly denies being a brand survey, and states that label reading cannot establish freedom from trace gluten via shared equipment.

No absolute safety guarantees anywhere, cross-contamination is raised in the body and repeated in two FAQ answers, and celiac risk is explicitly held to a stricter standard than the authors' own NCGS reality.
Both the manufacturer and regulatory citations carry a retrieval date, the standard is flagged as amended regularly, and reformulation without package redesign is named as a live risk.
The mandatory-allergen scope (wheat yes, barley and rye no), 밀떡 versus 쌀떡, dangmyeon as sweet potato starch, 양조간장 as wheat-fermented, and 집간장 as soybeans and salt are all described correctly.

The reader is given the exact Korean strings to scan for, a direct link to the regulatory standard and the manufacturer page, and a standing rule that the front label is where checking starts and the 원재료명 is where it finishes.

findings.quote: bound with wheat starch, nearly always
findings.why: The second-tier list states category-wide facts about eomuk, curry roux, sausages, dressings and fried-chicken batter without a source and without marking them as the authors' own label observations. The method paragraph only covers "the products we cook with," so these generalisations fall outside the stated basis. They err toward avoidance, so no reader is put at risk, but they are unverifiable as written.
findings.fix: Either attach one manufacturer or regulatory reference per category item, or add a half-sentence to the method block saying these defaults are general category knowledge rather than label-verified findings.

findings.quote: we learned to say **"밀가루 알러지"** (wheat allergy) rather than "gluten-free."
findings.why: The article correctly establishes that barley and rye are outside Korea's mandatory allergen line, but the restaurant script it recommends asks only about wheat. A celiac using that phrase would not surface barley-containing items such as malt syrup or 보리차 that the article itself names as real risks. Not blocking, since the barley gap is stated clearly elsewhere and the piece directs celiacs to home cooking.
findings.fix: Add barley to the spoken script for celiac readers, e.g. note that celiacs should also ask about 보리, since the wheat-allergy phrasing will not prompt staff to check barley-based ingredients.
